english: To whom do I give the charming new little book
just now polished with dry pumice?
Cornelius, to you; for you used
to think my trifles to be something,
note: nugae: trifles, Catullus's own word for his poems.

latin: iam tum cum ausus es unus Italorum
english: already then when you dared, alone of the Italians,
to unfold every age in three papers,
note: chartis: papyrus rolls, i.e. three volumes; Nepos's Chronica.

english: learned, by Jupiter, and laborious!

latin: quare habe tibi quidquid hoc libelli
english: therefore have for yourself whatever this is of a little book,
of whatever sort, which, O patron maiden,
note: patrona virgo: most likely the Muse (some take Minerva).

english: may remain lasting more than one age.
Sparrow, delight of my girl,

latin: quicum ludere, quem in sinu tenere,
english: with whom to play, whom in her lap to hold,
to whom, seeking, the first finger to give
note: primum digitum: the fingertip.

english: and sharp bites she is accustomed to provoke,
when to my shining desire
note: desiderio meo nitenti: the radiant object of my longing, i.e. the girl.

english: it pleases to joke some dear something-or-other
(and a little solace of her pain,

latin: credo, ut tum gravis adquiescat ardor),
english: I believe, so that then the heavy heat may rest),
with you to play just as she herself, could I
note: possem: wish, 'if only I could'.

english: and lighten the sad cares of the mind!

note: Gap marked in Merrill's text after line 10; lines 11-13 are printed by many editors as a separate fragment (2b). Merrill has no separate 2b record.

latin: Tam gratum est mihi quam ferunt puellae
english: As pleasing it is to me as they say to the girl
swift the golden little apple was,
note: pernici ... puellae: the swift girl, Atalanta, slowed by the golden apple.

english: which loosed the girdle long tied.
Mourn, O Venuses and Cupids,
and as much as there is of more charming people!
the sparrow is dead of my girl,
the sparrow, delight of my girl,

latin: quem plus illa oculis suis amabat;
english: whom more than her own eyes she loved;
for honey-sweet he was, and his own he knew,
note: suam ... ipsa: his own mistress herself.

latin: ipsa tam bene quam puella matrem,
english: herself, as well as a girl her mother,

english: nor from her lap did he move himself,

latin: sed circumsiliens modo huc modo illuc
english: but hopping around, now here now there,
to his mistress alone he kept cheeping.

latin: qui nunc it per iter tenebricosum
english: who now goes along the shadowy road
to there from where they deny anyone returns.

latin: at vobis male sit, malae tenebrae
english: but to you may it be badly, bad shadows
of Orcus, which devour all pretty things;
so pretty a sparrow you have taken away from me.

latin: o factum male! o miselle passer!
english: O deed done badly! O poor little sparrow!
by your doing now my girl's

That bean-boat, which you see, guests,
note: phasellus: a light, fast boat (named from the bean-pod shape); hospites: strangers, visitors.

english: says that it was of ships the swiftest,
nor of any swimming timber the onrush
was unable to pass, whether with little palms

english: there was need to fly or with linen.
note: linteo: sail.

english: And this it denies the menacing Adriatic's
note: negat ... negare: it denies that the shore denies; double negative left unresolved, i.e. the shore admits it.

english: shore to deny, or the Cycladic islands
note: negare: infinitive of indirect statement after negat (line 6), subject litus.

english: and noble Rhodes and rough Thrace,
Propontis or the fierce Pontic gulf,

latin: ubi iste post phasellus antea fuit
english: where that one, afterwards a bean-boat, before was

english: a long-haired forest: for on the Cytorian ridge

english: Pontic Amastris and box-bearing Cytorus,

latin: tibi haec fuisse et esse cognitissima
english: to you these things were and are most well-known,
says the bean-boat; from its furthest origin
on your peak it says it stood,
in your water it dipped its little palms,

latin: et inde tot per impotentia freta
english: and from there through so many unruly straits
carried its master, whether left or right
called the breeze, or both Jupiter
together favorable had fallen upon, the sheet;
note: utrumque ... in pedem: on both sheets at once (pes: sail-rope), i.e. wind dead astern.

english: nor any vows to the shore gods

latin: sibi esse facta, cum veniret a mari
english: by it had been made, when it came from the sea
note: Some editions read 'a mari' / 'a marei'; kept as in Merrill.

latin: novissimo hunc ad usque limpidum lacum.
english: the last, all the way to this clear lake.
note: novissimo: lit. newest, i.e. the last (furthest) sea.

latin: sed haec prius fuere: nunc recondita
english: But these things were before: now, put away,
it grows old in quiet and dedicates itself to you,
twin Castor and twin of Castor.
Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love,
and the rumors of the more severe old men
all let us value at one as.
note: assis: genitive of value of as, the smallest copper coin.

english: Suns can set and return:

latin: nobis, cum semel occidit brevis lux,
english: for us, when once has set the brief light,
night perpetual, one, is to be slept.
note: est ... dormienda: gerundive with est, 'must be slept'; perpetua una agree with nox.

latin: da mi basia mille, deinde centum,
english: Give me kisses a thousand, then a hundred,

latin: dein mille altera, dein secunda centum,
english: then another thousand, then a second hundred,

latin: deinde usque altera mille, deinde centum,
english: then still another thousand, then a hundred,
then, when many thousands we shall have made,
we shall throw them into confusion, so that we do not know,
note: conturbabimus: accounting term, to jumble the accounts (also, to go bankrupt).

latin: aut ne quis malus invidere possit,
english: or so that no bad one can envy,
note: invidere: also 'cast the evil eye on'.

english: when he knows so many there are of kisses.
Flavius, your delights to Catullus,
unless they be uncharming and inelegant,
note: sint: present subjunctive, kept against the imperfect subjunctives velles, posses of line 3.

english: you would want to tell, nor could you be silent.
But some feverish something-or-other
of a whore you love: this you are ashamed to confess.
note: pudet: impersonal, 'it shames [you]'.

latin: nam te non viduas iacere noctes
english: For that you do not lie through widowed nights
in vain silent the bed cries out,
note: nequiquam goes with tacitum: the bed, silent to no purpose, cries out [that you do not lie alone].

english: with garlands and Syrian olive-oil fragrant,

latin: pulvinusque peraeque et hic et ille
english: and the pillow, equally both this one and that,
worn down, and of the trembling bed the shaken
creaking and walking-about.
note: inambulatio: the bed's 'walking about', its moving across the floor.

latin: nam nil stupra valet, nihil, tacere.
english: For nothing avails, nothing, to keep silent about debaucheries.
note: Textually doubtful line; Merrill prints 'nam nil stupra valet, nihil, tacere' (other editors read 'nam inista prevalet' or 'ista vales'). Rendered as printed: stupra is object of tacere, 'to keep silent about debaucheries'.

latin: cur? non tam latera ecfututa pandas,
english: Why? You would not spread out flanks so fucked-out,
note: latera ecfututa: flanks worn out by fucking.

english: unless you were doing something of follies.
Therefore, whatever you have of good and bad,

latin: dic nobis: volo te ac tuos amores
english: tell us: I want you and your loves
to the sky with charming verse to call.
You ask how many kissings to me
of yours, Lesbia, are enough and more than enough.
As great as the number of Libyan sand
note: harenae: sand (grains).

english: lies at silphium-bearing Cyrene,
note: laserpiciferis: bearing laserpicium, silphium.

english: between the oracle of sweltering Jove
note: Iovis aestuosi: Jupiter Ammon, in the hot desert.

english: and the sacred tomb of old Battus,

latin: aut quam sidera multa, cum tacet nox,
english: or as many as the stars, when night is silent,
see the stolen loves of men,
so many kisses you to kiss

latin: vesano satis et super Catullo est,

which neither to count up the curious

english: could, nor a bad tongue bewitch.
note: fascinare: to cast the evil eye, bewitch.

english: Wretched Catullus, you should stop being foolish,

latin: et quod vides perisse perditum ducas.
english: and what you see has perished, count as lost.
Shone once bright suns for you,
when you kept coming where the girl led,
loved by us as much as will be loved none.

latin: ibi illa multa tum iocosa fiebant,
english: There those many playful things then happened,

latin: quae tu volebas nec puella nolebat.
english: which you wanted, and the girl did not not-want.
note: nec ... nolebat: was not unwilling.

english: Shone truly bright suns for you.

latin: nunc iam illa non vult: tu quoque, impotens, noli,
english: Now already she does not want: you too, powerless, do not want,
note: impotens: without self-control.

latin: nec quae fugit sectare, nec miser vive,
english: nor her who flees chase, nor live wretched,
note: quae: feminine singular, the girl; sectare: deponent imperative.

english: but with obstinate mind endure, be hard.
Farewell, girl! Already Catullus is hard,

latin: nec te requiret nec rogabit invitam:
english: and will not seek you nor ask you unwilling:

latin: at tu dolebis, cum rogaberis nulla.
english: but you will grieve, when you are asked not at all.
note: rogaberis nulla: lit. 'you will be asked, none', i.e. not asked at all.

latin: scelesta, vae te! quae tibi manet vita!
english: Wicked one, woe to you! What life remains for you!
note: scelesta: also 'wretched one'; vae te: accusative with vae.

latin: quis nunc te adibit? cui videberis bella?
english: Who now will approach you? To whom will you seem pretty?

latin: quem nunc amabis? cuius esse diceris?
english: Whom now will you love? Whose will you be said to be?
Whom will you kiss? Whose little lips will you bite?
But you, Catullus, determined, be hard.
Veranius, of all my friends
standing before for me by three hundred thousands,
note: antistans ... milibus trecentis: surpassing by three hundred thousand.

english: have you come home to your household gods
and like-minded brothers and old mother?
You have come! O for me blessed news!
I shall see you unharmed and shall hear, of the Spaniards,
note: Hiberum: genitive plural, of the Hiberians (Spaniards).

english: narrating places, deeds, nations,
note: narrantem: agrees with te (line 6).

latin: ut mos est tuus, applicansque collum
english: as is your custom, and drawing close your neck
your delightful mouth and eyes I shall kiss.
O, as much as there is of more blessed men,
what is happier than me or more blessed?

latin: Varus me meus ad suos amores
english: Varus, my one, me to his love
to see had led from the forum, idle,

latin: scortillum, ut mihi tunc repente visum est,
english: a little whore, as it seemed to me then suddenly,
not really uncharming nor unlovely.
When we came here, there fell to us

latin: sermones varii, in quibus, quid esset
english: various conversations, among which, what was

english: now Bithynia, in what way it was keeping,
note: se haberet: how it was faring.

english: whether with any money it had profited me.
note: aere: bronze, money.

latin: respondi id quod erat, nihil neque ipsis
english: I answered that which was so: nothing, neither for themselves

english: nor for the praetors to be, nor for the staff,

english: why anyone should bring back his head more oiled,

english: "But surely all the same," they say, "what there

english: I might make myself the one more fortunate,
note: unum ... beatiorem: the one luckier man.

english: "Not," I say, "did it go so badly for me,
that, because a bad province had befallen,

english: I could not get eight straight men."

Here she, as befitted a rather catamite-like one,

english: be carried." "Wait," I said to the girl,

my reasoning escaped me: my comrade

english: But whether his or mine, what is it to me?

english: I use them as well as if I had acquired them for myself.

Furius and Aurelius, companions of Catullus,
whether into the furthest Indians he will penetrate,
where the shore by the far-resounding Eastern

or into the Hyrcanians or soft Arabs,
or Sacae or arrow-bearing Parthians,
or which the sevenfold colors

visiting the monuments of great Caesar,
the Gallic Rhine, the horrible water, the furth-

english: -est and Britons,
all these, whatever the will will bring

With her adulterers let her live and fare well,

english: whom at once embracing she holds, three hundred,

english: loving none truly, but again and again of all
the groins bursting;
note: ilia rumpens: rupturing their groins (ilia: flanks, loins), i.e. draining them sexually.

latin: nec meum respectet, ut ante, amorem,
english: nor let her look back to my love, as before,

english: which by her fault has fallen like of the meadow
furthest, the flower, after by the passing

english: plough it has been touched.
Marrucinian Asinius, the left hand

note: lintea: linen napkins.

note: Source runs 'mihi?crede' together; Latin kept exactly.

english: your brother, who your thefts even for a talent

english: to be exchanged would want; for he is of wit

Therefore either hendecasyllables three hundred
expect, or send me back the napkin,
which moves me not by its value,
but is a keepsake of my comrade.
note: mnemosynum: Greek loanword, memento.

english: For Saetaban handkerchiefs from the Spaniards
note: Saetaba: from Saetabis in Spain, famed for linen.

english: sent me as a gift Fabullus

latin: et Veranius: haec amem necesse est
english: and Veranius: these I must love,
and my little Veranius and Fabullus.
note: et ... et as printed by Merrill: 'both these and ...'; other editions read 'ut' (as I love).

latin: Cenabis bene, mi Fabulle, apud me
english: You will dine well, my Fabullus, at my place

english: in a few, if the gods favor you, days,

english: if with you you bring a good and big
dinner, not without a fair girl
note: candida: bright, fair, radiant.

latin: et vino et sale et omnibus cachinnis.
english: and wine and salt and all laughs.
note: sale: salt, also wit.

latin: haec si, inquam, attuleris, venuste noster
english: These if, I say, you bring, our charming one,
you will dine well; for your Catullus's
little purse is full of cobwebs.
But in return you will receive pure loves
note: meros amores: unmixed love; also 'the very essence of love'.

english: or whatever is sweeter or more elegant:

latin: nam unguentum dabo, quod meae puellae
english: for an unguent I will give, which to my girl
note: unguentum: perfumed ointment; rendered literally, though some readers take it as the girl's own scent.

english: gave the Venuses and Cupids,

latin: quod tu cum olfacies, deos rogabis
english: which you, when you smell it, the gods you will ask
note: olfacies: 'it' is not in the Latin but the object is understood from quod.

latin: totum ut te faciant, Fabulle, nasum.
english: that they make you all, Fabullus, nose.
